title: Senior's toolkit: objects and arrays
summary: The built-in APIs experienced developers use to copy, reshape, group and inspect data without mutating it by accident.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: objects and arrays
steps.body: Most front-end and Node bugs with data are one of two things: something was mutated that should not have been, or the data was never looked at properly. These built-ins (all in Node 22 and every current browser) prevent both.

toolkit.what: A real deep copy. Spread (`{ ...obj }`) copies only the top level, so nested arrays and objects stay shared.
flags: plain objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays, even cycles
when the value holds a function
come back as plain objects, without their methods
toolkit.example:
const draft = structuredClone(order);
draft.lines.push(newLine); // order.lines is untouched

toolkit.what: The non-mutating twins (ES2023): `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with`. They return a new array, which is what React state and shared data need.
flags: numeric sort; without a compare function items are sorted as strings
a copy with one element replaced
toolkit.example: const byPrice = items.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price);

toolkit.what: Turn an object into `[key, value]` pairs, transform them with array methods, and turn them back with `Object.fromEntries`.
flags: just the keys or just the values
pairs (or a `Map`) back into an object
toolkit.example:
const doubled = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(prices).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * 2]));

toolkit.what: Group an array by a key in one call (ES2024), instead of a hand-written `reduce`.
flags: string keys, returns a null-prototype object of arrays

toolkit.what: Use `Map` for lookups with any key type and a reliable `size`, and `Set` for uniqueness. A plain object as a dictionary has inherited keys and only string keys.
toolkit.example:
const counts = new Map<string, number>();
for (const w of words) counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1);

toolkit.what: Pretty-print data for a log or a test failure. The third argument is the indent.
flags: a replacer array keeps only these keys
a method an object can define to control its own output

toolkit.what: See an array of objects as a table in the terminal or the browser console, so a wrong value stands out.

steps.prompt: A reviewer says the sort is wrong. What does this print?
steps.explain: Without a compare function, `sort` converts items to strings and sorts them as text, so `"10"` comes before `"9"`. Always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers. `sort` also mutates the array; `toSorted` does not.

steps.prompt: A bug report: after the user edits a draft order and presses Cancel, the original order still shows the edited tags. The draft was made with `const draft = { ...order }` and the edit was `draft.tags.push(tag)`. What is the fix?
options: Make the draft with `structuredClone(order)`: spread copies only the top level, so `tags` was the same array
Freeze the order with `Object.freeze(order)` so pushes are ignored
Use `let` instead of `const` for the draft
steps.explain: `Object.assign` is also a shallow copy. `Object.freeze` is shallow too, and would not stop `tags.push`. A deep copy (or building a new `tags` array with `[...draft.tags, tag]`) fixes it.

steps.prompt: Match each call to what it gives you.
pairs: a sorted copy, the original untouched
an object of arrays, one per key

steps.prompt: Apply a 10% discount to every price in an object and get an object back.
steps.explain: `Object.entries` gives `[key, value]` pairs to map over; `Object.fromEntries` turns the pairs back into an object.

steps.prompt: Does the call change the original array, or return a new one?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When data is shared (React state, a cache, a function's arguments), reach for the non-mutating method or `structuredClone` first, and treat `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` as a review question. When something looks wrong, `console.table` it before you start reasoning about it.
